name: Kyoto Tycoon
tagline: FAL Labs' HTTP and memcached-speaking network server for Kyoto Cabinet, with expiry and replication.
description: Kyoto Tycoon is the network front end to the Kyoto Cabinet DBM library, written in C++ by Mikio Hirabayashi's FAL Labs from 2010. A single server process hosts multiple hash or B+tree databases, in memory or on disk, and clients talk to it over a RESTful/RPC HTTP protocol, a compact binary protocol or a memcached-compatible plug-in. Records can carry expiration times, so it doubles as a persistent cache, and it supports master-slave and dual-master replication via update logs plus server-side Lua scripting. Development stopped with 0.9.56 in 2012; Cloudflare ran it for years for edge configuration before replacing it with Quicksilver, and Altice Labs kept a fork that is now archived. The author's successor is Tkrzw-RPC.
statusNote: No upstream release since 0.9.56 (April 2012); community forks (Altice Labs, Cloudflare) are archived. The author's successor is Tkrzw with Tkrzw-RPC.

scale.notes: One server per node; replication is log shipping to slaves or a dual-master pair; sharding is client-side.

strengths: Very fast hash and B+tree storage inherited from Kyoto Cabinet
Per-record expiration makes it a persistent cache
Speaks HTTP, a binary protocol and the memcached protocol
Master-slave and dual-master replication via update logs
weaknesses: Hard to operate at scale: one process per database file, awkward upgrades
No built-in sharding or consensus-based failover
useCases: Legacy caches and config stores still running it
Studying a compact C++ KV server design
notIdealFor: New deployments (use Redis/Valkey, or Tkrzw-RPC for the same lineage)
Systems that need automatic failover or sharding
